svg.title: Offset: the reading when the wheel points straight
svg.desc: Animated. Left, a steering module with its wheel squared to a straight-edge. Right, a dial: the encoder's raw reading points off at a random angle even though the wheel points straight, because the encoder was mounted at a random angle. That reading is the offset, drawn as an arc. Subtracting it swings the code's angle back to zero. Then the wheel steers and both needles turn together, the offset arc riding between them: raw minus offset is the angle the code uses. Below, drawn to scale, a path one degree off drifts about 2 in over 10 ft. Capture offsets with every wheel squared to a straight-edge, all bevel gears facing the same way. Copied or rounded offsets are the most common swerve fault.
svg.text: Offset: the reading when the wheel points straight
Each encoder is mounted at a random angle, so the code needs to know where 'straight' is.

g.text: 1. Wheel straight: the raw reading is the offset.
2. Subtract the offset: straight now reads 0.
3. Steer: raw − offset follows the wheel.

svg.text: offset: the raw reading at straight
raw − offset: the angle the code uses
Why it matters: one degree wrong is about 2 in of drift per 10 ft.
Capture them with every wheel squared to a straight-edge,
all bevel gears facing the same way.
Copied or rounded offsets are the most common swerve fault.
